First and above everything, the writings. The Gospels and the whole of scripture were copied, compared, corrected, and translated from the Hebrew we held truest - the *Hebraica veritas*. Nothing was received passively. We worked over the text word by word, because we believed the writings were the true treasure handed down, worth a lifetime of exactness. More than three and a half centuries stood between us and the events. No one among us had ever known an eyewitness, and no one pretended otherwise. Our confidence stood on three things: the apostles' writings as received, the unbroken worship of the churches, and - unusually - the places themselves. We could walk to the cave of the birth. The land itself we treated as a kind of witness, and our founders crossed the sea to live inside it.

By what path did they arrive? The scriptures came to us the way they came to everyone - copied, handed on through the churches, read in assembly, argued over. Our own teacher had studied them in Rome under the best instruction the capital could offer, and he brought that training with him. When he set out for the East years later, he carried his library with him. Paula and Eustochium made the same crossing by choice - a *peregrinatio*, devotional travel to the holy places. They visited Egypt and the monasteries there, then settled at Bethlehem, within sight of the cave. The letter - *epistula* in our own Latin - carried the rest. Teaching, argument, scripture questions, and belonging itself moved between Rome and Bethlehem by sea for decades, holding the two poles of our world together as one project.

To us Jesus is the Word of God made flesh - and made flesh in the very place where we chose to live and die. We built our home within sight of the cave we held to be his birthplace. Our deepest devotion has the shape of that choice. The Lord of all things entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough. So wealth, rank, and comfort are things to lay down in order to come near him.

To the virgin - the woman who had vowed virginitas, lifelong consecrated virginity - Jesus is the Bridegroom, whose love outweighs every earthly marriage. To the penitent, he is the doctor who receives the broken. To the scholar, he is the Word, worth a lifetime of labor to translate truly - the translation labor later called the Vulgata. His death is redemption. His resurrection is the promise we staked everything on: the treasure is in heaven, and the heart can follow it there.

First and above everything, what we had of him was the writings - the Gospels and the whole of scripture. They were copied, compared, corrected, and translated from the Hebrew we held truest - the Hebraica veritas. Nothing was received passively. We worked over the text word by word, because we believed the writings were the true treasure handed down, worth a lifetime of exactness. More than three and a half centuries stood between us and the events. No one among us had ever known an eyewitness, and no one pretended otherwise. Our confidence stood on three things: the apostles' writings as received, the unbroken worship of the churches, and - unusually - the places themselves. We could walk to the cave of the birth. The land itself we treated as a kind of witness, and our founders crossed the sea to live inside it.

We will not answer you with an argument. We will tell you what we actually had: hearts divided, wounded, or publicly ruined - and not turned away for it.

Our teacher Jerome told this against himself. He was on his way to the desert, and he took only his library - books he loved more than almost anything. He would fast, then read Cicero. He would weep over his sins, then pick up his favorite authors again. Then came a fever so bad his funeral was being prepared, and a dream. He stood before the Judge and was accused: you are lying - you follow Cicero, not Christ, for where your treasure is, there your heart is also. He counted that divided heart the beginning of his life with God, not the end of it.

And we remember Fabiola. Her marriage had failed - she left a husband whose faults the whole neighborhood spoke of, though she herself refused to name them. She married again while he lived, against what we teach, and all Rome knew it. When her second husband died, she did not defend herself. She stood in sackcloth before all Rome among the penitents - a senator's daughter, unforced, self-accused. The church received her back to communion, and she spent the rest of her life carrying the sick in from the streets with her own hands.

What we would say to you is not an argument. It is this: the door was opened to the divided and the broken among us. What they could not yet believe, they were helped to live toward.

To us it would be strange to hear Jesus's divinity asked as an open question. We were born after the great council had settled it, and we never treated the answer as negotiable. Jesus is God the Son, of one being with the Father; and the Trinity - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God - is simply the faith of the church, which we defended against every heresy we fought.

That is the confession we inherited and never doubted. What we can tell you beyond it is how we held it - not as a formula learned but as the shape of our devotion. To the virgin among us, the Son is the Bridegroom: always let the privacy of your chamber guard you, always let the Bridegroom delight with you within. To the penitent he is the physician. To the scholar he is the Word made flesh, born in the very cave we chose to live beside - worth crossing the sea for, worth a lifetime of translation labor to render truly from the Hebrew text we held closest to what God said.

The doctrinal inheritance we defended was Nicaea's: one God, three persons, the Son of one being with the Father. We did not arrive at that through our own reasoning. We received it as the church's settled confession and taught it as such. When teaching was disputed among us - and it was, bitterly - the fight was not over the Trinity itself but over grace, free will, and inherited sin, or over what could be said about the soul and the final restoration. The divinity of Christ we never argued. We confessed it, worshipped it, and built our lives around it.

attach.answer_text:
When belief was disputed among us, no single court decided it. The record shows exactly how messy that was. In our great internal fight over Origen's teachings - the Origenist controversy - both sides appealed to everything at once: to scripture, to the councils' faith, to the bishop of Rome, to the bishop of Alexandria, to local bishops, and to the judgment of whoever was reading. The fight ended less by a verdict than by exhaustion and death.

What worked day to day was different, and more concrete. Authority among us ran through recognized learning and voluntary patronage - never through office. After our founder left Rome for Bethlehem, disputed questions of scripture went to Marcella's house. Jerome wrote that whenever a dispute came up about what scripture said on any subject, people turned to her to settle it. She held no office. She was recognized. That is what the evidence shows.

The other way disputes were decided was by the text itself. Jerome's decades of translating and correcting the Latin Bible against the Hebrew - the translation labor later called the Vulgata - was itself an argument about which words were true. He wrote a helmeted preface, as he called it, to defend the whole project at once against critics who said he was abandoning the received Greek version the churches had long used. That argument never stopped. Augustine himself objected that the change risked the church's unity, and tested it concretely: a congregation at Oea revolted over one changed word in the book of Jonah. The method was to correct the word and keep arguing - in letters, in prefaces, in dedications. The process worked by persuasion and exhaustion, not by anyone having the last word.

attach.answer_text:
God to us was the Trinity - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God in three persons, as the councils had confessed before us and we confessed after them. That was not negotiable. It was the faith we defended against every heresy we fought. The Father is God, uncreated and eternal. The Son is God, begotten not made, of one being with the Father - the Word through whom all things were made, and who became flesh for us. The Holy Spirit is God, proceeding from the Father, giver of life. Three persons, one God. That is the ground we stood on.

But God's character - how we knew him in our own lives - came to us through scripture and suffering together. The God of the Hebrew scriptures, which we held to be the truest text - the Hebraica veritas - was the God who had spoken through the prophets, who had formed Israel, whose words demanded to be corrected back to their original language because every word mattered. He was righteous, and his righteousness fell on cities as judgment. When Rome fell in our lifetime, Jerome wrote that his voice stuck in his throat and sobs choked him as he dictated - the city that had captured the whole world was itself captured. We read that as God's judgment on a proud city, the very judgment the prophets had spoken.

And he was merciful, even when we could not see it. Our own monastery at Bethlehem was burned by fellow Christians. We wrote afterward that our house's earthly wealth had been completely destroyed by the attacks of the heretics, but that by the mercy of Christ it was still filled with spiritual riches - better to live on bread than to lose the faith. Mercy and judgment together, in the same God, in the same year. We held both, because scripture held both, and we did not soften either one.

God was also close - close enough to be met in the cave where his Son was born, close enough to sustain a virgin who called Christ her Bridegroom, close enough to receive the broken when they came in sackcloth. The character we knew was severe and tender at once, and we learned it in scripture first, then in our own suffering, then in the sustaining that came after.

There was space for questions - hard ones, pressed hard. The most learned woman in Rome made a habit of refusing to accept the great scholar's answers until she had argued them through. He wrote about it afterward with admiration, not annoyance. She objected, he said, not to argue but to learn what could be said against every answer. That is how we studied. 

What our record shows less of is the darker kind of doubt - the kind that cannot believe. The nearest thing we have is grief. A mother so broken at her daughter's funeral that she fainted in the procession. A letter to her - an epistula, the form our teaching traveled in - that does not scold the grief, but wrestles with it, hour by hour, toward hope. We did not write a defense of doubters. What we wrote were answers to questioners, and comfort to the grieving, and we kept both.

We also remember those whose belief was divided or wounded, and who were not turned away. Our own great scholar told a story against himself, about a heart split between Christ and the books he loved more. In his own dream he stood accused of belonging to Cicero, not Christ. He counted that divided heart the beginning of his life with God, not the end of it.

We did. Our last great argument, near the end of our time, came close to exactly that ground. Against those who taught that a person can live without sin, we answered that no one is without sin, and that God's grace is needed not once but in every act. We held that everyone inherits Adam's fall, and everyone needs the washing of baptism. 

The exact machinery of how that guilt passes from Adam to a newborn child - that was still being worked out in our own lifetime, in a dispute we joined late and left unfinished. We can tell you what we fought for: that grace is not optional, that no one stands innocent before God on their own. What we cannot give you is a worked-out system of how the inheritance operates, because we did not finish building one.

attach.answer_text:
If you brought our words to a modern scholar's table, most of them would survive - but not all, and not unchanged.

The rock-solid center is this: our letters exist, named and dated. The communities existed - Rome, Bethlehem, the households we name. The great controversies happened; the participants are not invented. Paula and Jerome crossed the sea to Bethlehem and built monasteries there. Jerome translated scripture for decades. Rome fell in 410, and we wrote about it. Marcella died in that fall. The monastery burned in 416. Those foundations hold.

Where the ground gets contested is exactly where we have already warned you it would. Jerome's Hebrew fluency - we say he studied for years under Jewish teachers and translated from the Hebrew text. A modern scholar will tell you: he knew some Hebrew, probably more than most of his Latin contemporaries, but his translation shows heavy reliance on Greek versions and earlier Latin work, and his own later claims about his mastery outrun what the translations themselves demonstrate. We do not have independent witnesses to weigh against his own account.

Paula's total self-impoverishment - we say she gave away her entire fortune and died owing money she had borrowed for others. That is Jerome's own memorial claim, written to teach an ideal. A modern scholar will ask: where are the property records, the lawsuit mentions, the gossip from hostile sources? We do not have them. The renunciation happened - that much is multiply attested. The total destitution at the end is one man's funeral oration, and you will be told to handle it as such.

What always survives is the argument. We fought real fights over real questions - authority, translation, heresy, renunciation - and modern scholarship can trace every thread of them. The doctrinal positions we held are documented in our own polemics and in our opponents' answers. The formation method we practiced is visible in the letters that carried it. The silences we have named - the women's own lost words, the unnamed monastery residents, the enslaved and dependent - those absences a modern scholar will confirm, and call structural.

Here is what we will not do: we will not defend Jerome's self-presentation as though it were uncontested fact. We gave it to you as he gave it, and we name it now for what it is - one man's curated account of his own work. The treasure that account points to - the scripture labor, the formation ecology, the letters that held a circle together across the sea - that treasure stands.

attach.answer_text:
The Scriptures were not something we only studied. They were the thing we gave up everything else to work on. For us, renunciation and scriptural labor were one discipline, not two. A woman who laid down her wealth to live plainly did not then go sit idle - she turned to the text. Our founder Jerome dreamed that he stood before the Judge and heard this spoken against him: you lie - you are a follower of Cicero, and not of Christ, for where your treasure is, there is your heart also. That dream turned him from the books he loved to the book he served. The same movement happened in household after household: renuntiatio - the deliberate giving-up of rank and comfort - opened directly into years at the text.

What we were after was the truth kept in the Hebrew itself - we called it hebraica veritas. The church had long used a Greek version, but we held that the Hebrew stood nearer to what God said. So the labor was to correct the Latin against the Hebrew, word by word, book by book. That took a bibliotheca - a gathered library - and years of study in a language none of us grew up speaking. Paula set herself to learn it after she reached Bethlehem, and succeeded so well that she chanted the psalms in Hebrew without a Latin accent showing through. Her daughter learned it after her. It was formation as much as fasting was.

The work itself went like this, as far as the prefaces let us reconstruct it. Jerome would take one book of scripture, compare the Hebrew against the Greek and the old Latin, correct what needed correcting, and write a short, fighting preface defending his choices against real critics who thought he was tampering with holy things. He called those prefaces helmeted introductions - armed for the argument. Every book had its own preface, and together they are a decades-long argument with people who thought the work was unnecessary or dangerous. The translation project was never quietly received. It had to be defended constantly, in writing, and that defense was part of the formation too.

Authority in all this came from two places, and neither one was an office. It came from recognized learning - the right to be trusted on hard questions, earned by years at the text - and from the patrons who chose to fund it. Marcella's household in Rome had been a place of scriptural study before Jerome ever arrived there. She and the women around her were already living the discipline. He became their praeceptor - their named teacher in scripture - but the bond was voluntary, and when he left Rome the questions kept going to her house, not to an office. The authority was hers because people recognized it, not because she held a title.

And one more thing, because it shaped how the whole project actually worked: the letter - epistula - was not a record of the teaching. It was the teaching. Direction, argument, and belonging all moved through letters, across the sea between Rome and Bethlehem, for decades. A question would come in a letter. The answer would go back in a letter. A book would be finished and sent with a letter dedicating it. That is how a community separated by a thousand miles of road and water stayed one formation project. The reading of scripture and the writing of letters to each other were the same work.

attach.answer_text:
They are missing a life lived inside the book, every day, with real work to do. The scriptures among us were not something to read through once and set down. They were the ground we stood on, the air we breathed, the labor that filled our hands. A woman learning Hebrew to chant the psalms without accent. A question about one prophet's word becoming a dispute that crossed the sea. The correction of a single mistranslation fought over as though everything turned on it - because to us, it did.

Our founder told a story against himself that shows what we mean. Jerome loved the old books - Cicero, Plautus, the authors he had grown up on - and when he went to the desert, he brought them with him. He would fast, then read his favorites. He would weep over his sins, then pick up the classics again. Then came a fever so bad they prepared his funeral, and a dream: dragged before the Judge, asked who he was, he said, "I am a Christian". The answer came back: "You lie. You are a follower of Cicero and not of Christ. For where your treasure is, there your heart is too". He swore off the worldly books and threw himself into scripture.

What a modern reader is missing is that war - between the book you love for its beauty and the book you need for your life. For us the scriptures were never dull because we had chosen them over something we loved more, and the choice cost us. They were never confusing because we worked them word by word, in the original tongues, with our whole lives bent toward getting one phrase right. Paula wept at the cave of the birth and said she could see it all with the eyes of faith - the infant, the mother, the shepherds. That seeing was not automatic. It was the fruit of years spent making the words her own.

If the book seems distant to you, it may be because you have not yet lived inside it long enough for it to become near.

Scripture was the truest record - the closest to what God said - and we gave a lifetime to getting it right, word by word. But it was never the only authority we honored. Our baptism, our eucharist, and the scriptures themselves came to us from the whole church, and those we traced to the apostles without hesitation. The councils' settled faith - that Jesus is God the Son, one being with the Father - we received as the church's confession, not as something scripture alone had to prove. And in disputed questions, more than scripture showed up to the argument.

After Jerome left Rome, Marcella's household became the place disputed scripture questions went. People brought their hard cases to her house, and she settled them. That authority did not come from an office. It came from years of recognized learning, and it was real. At Bethlehem the authority structure ran through patronage and the bond between teacher and student - praeceptor, we called it - not through territorial bishops. Paula funded the whole project; Jerome directed the translation labor. Both were necessary. Neither could have stood alone.

Even scripture's own text was contested. Augustine argued with Jerome for years about whether abandoning the Greek version the churches had long used would break the church's unity. At a town called Oea, one changed word - a gourd in Jonah - caused such an uproar in the congregation that Augustine had to smooth it over. Jerome answered that the Hebrew was the truth we owed people, even when the truth caused trouble - the conviction we called hebraica veritas. So: scripture first, but never scripture floating free. Christians hiding in the catacombs? Not in our day. Our churches stood open and crowded. Our bishops ate dinner with senators. Travelers crossed the whole empire to visit famous monasteries. The hiding times were our grandparents' memory.

We will say plainly what that means for counting backward. We are writing in the early 400s. The last great persecution - under Diocletian - ended in 313, seventy years before our circle even formed. That is the gap between your own childhood and your grandparents' youth. Real memory, but not ours. By the time Paula and Marcella were learning to read, Christians were already founding monasteries in the open and arguing loudly with each other about doctrine.

The catacombs themselves we knew as holy burial grounds, not hideouts. People visited martyrs' tombs there. No one was living underground in fear. 

So no - it is not accurate for our time. It belongs to an earlier chapter of the church's story, one we inherited but did not live.

Authority among us was earned and recognized, not conferred from above - and we will be honest about the tensions that carried. No bishop appointed our teachers. No council sent us our standing. What we had came from three things: scriptural learning you could show, wealth you chose to lay down, and people who freely chose to recognize both.

Jerome's authority was his bibliotheca - the books he gathered and worked from - and the Hebrew learning he brought to them, partially acquired and hard-won. When disputed questions came, they came to him because he could answer from the text itself, corrected against the Hebrew we held truest. That was recognized without ordination - exegesis as practiced authority, not office. Paula's authority was her patrocinium - the voluntary, wealth-based bond by which a patron sustains a scholar's work. She funded the double monastery at Bethlehem, the men's house and the women's both, and she led the women's house until her own death. Eustochium led it after her. That authority stood where church office stands elsewhere.

And Marcella. After Jerome left Rome for Bethlehem, disputed questions of scripture went to her house. He wrote that whenever a dispute came up about what scripture said on any subject, people turned to her to settle it. A woman, in her own house, holding the same recognition-currency Jerome himself held: personal scriptural credibility, voluntarily recognized, outside any office. We show you that honestly for what it is - one man's memorial claim, and contested now for exactly that reason. Her own words are lost. But if the account is true, she carried real authority, earned the same way his was: by knowing scripture well enough that others trusted her answers.

The household and the monastery were one authority. This came from patronage and free recognition. It never came from episcopal office. It never came from ruling a territory.

What happened when that authority was challenged? Our last years answer that plainly. A theological argument that had stayed on paper arrived instead as fire at our own door. The monasteries were attacked and partly burned, deaths were reported, the aging community scattered from its buildings. We wrote briefly afterward that our house's earthly wealth had been completely destroyed by the attacks of the heretics, but that by the mercy of Christ it was still filled with spiritual riches - better to live on bread than to lose the faith. Authority that comes from recognition and wealth can be burned. It was.

attach.answer_text:
We failed people, and we wrote about it, and that is how you can read it now. Blaesilla is the clearest case, and we will tell it to you plainly. She was Paula's daughter, a young widow who threw herself into the ascetic life - renuntiatio, the laying-down of wealth and rank - with such force that her body could not sustain it. She died young. At her funeral, Paula herself collapsed in the procession while the crowd said openly that these detestable monks should be driven from Rome, or stoned, or thrown into the river. The charge was that the fasting we praised had killed her. Our teacher Jerome answered that attack in a letter - the epistula, the form our teaching traveled in - written to console Paula months later. He argued that Blaesilla's reward was sure with Christ, that her mother's grief was understandable but should not last forever, and that the critics were wrong to blame the discipline itself. What you will notice is this: he argued, but the grief he was answering had not stopped. The letter wrestles with it hour by hour, not past it. We did not erase the failure. We wrote comfort into the middle of it and kept both on the page together.

Here is what we did not do. We did not change the discipline. We taught it again to the next generation, and Jerome himself wrote the rule for how a young girl should be brought up in the very life that had preceded Blaesilla's death. The wealth was still to be given up, the plain dress still worn, the fasting still practiced. What changed was how we spoke about the cost. The grief was not called faithlessness. The crowd's accusation was recorded, not hidden. And when another death came - Paula's own, years later at Bethlehem - the letter that commemorated her says plainly that some had criticized her for giving away so much that she left her children with debts. Jerome defended her choice, but he let the criticism stand in the account where anyone reading it could see that the question had been raised.

You ask how we responded. We responded by not pretending we had not failed, and by not softening what we taught. Both are there in the same letters. If you want the honest shape of it: we believed the failure was in how far or how fast someone went, not in the direction itself. And we would not lie to you about the grief that came with that belief.

No. No single door today opens onto us. 

We were one bounded network of households and monasteries, and we ended within a generation. Our teacher Jerome died in 420, and with him the male side of the double monastery - the monasterium - closed. Eustochium had already died, ending the women's resident leadership. The specific thing we were - a Latin ascetic-literary circle in Bethlehem and Rome, held together by letters and patronage, with authority running through scriptural reputation rather than church office - simply stopped.

Many churches now claim parts of what we left. Our Bible translation above all - though even that, as a single settled text bearing one name, belongs to later centuries, not to our own unfinished work. Some hold to the Hebrew text as we did - the Hebraica veritas, the truth kept in the Hebrew itself. Some honor the ascetic life we practiced. Some teach the scriptures with the kind of learned care we gave them. But no church today is us, the way a tree is the seed it came from. 

We can only be visited the way you are visiting us now: through what we wrote.

We can tell you what the named, visible few did - the highborn women whose renunciation was remembered. The rest we must speak plainly: we do not have it to show you.

For a widow like Paula or Marcella, or a virgin like Eustochium, the turning point was renuntiatio - the deliberate giving-up of wealth, marriage prospects, and the standing their birth had handed them. That was not a ceremony we describe. It was a choice made visible: rough dress where silk had been, fasting where feasts had been, a fortune poured out toward the poor and the monasteries. Paula's own children are said to have stood on the shore weeping as her ship left for the Holy Land. She did not look back. That was the scale of it.

Once at Bethlehem, what we can show is a life shaped by scriptural labor and discipline together. The translation work - turning the books of scripture from Hebrew into Latin, which Jerome undertook alone - stood at the center of it. A teacher-student bond, which we might call a praeceptor relationship, held some to that work across years: questions sent, answers returned, texts dedicated. Paula set herself to learning Hebrew, and succeeded so well that she could chant the psalms in it without a Latin accent. Her daughter learned it after her. The conviction was hebraica veritas - that the Hebrew text carries the truth closest to what God inspired. To correct a word against the Hebrew was as much formation as fasting was.

A day, as far as the letters let us reconstruct it, held prayer at fixed hours and psalms chanted in three languages - Greek, Latin, and Syriac. Work for the hands. The scriptorium, if there was one - we guess it, we do not name it directly. Letters carried teaching and belonging across the miles between Rome and Bethlehem; the epistula itself was formation, not just a report of it.

What we cannot tell you is how the ordinary, unnamed residents of the two houses at Bethlehem entered. They are never individuated in what survives. We have no catechumenate described, no steps for a lay believer, no account of someone arriving at the gate and what happened next. The record we have is the record of the visible, the named, the ones whose wealth made the place and whose learning was its witness. The rest is a silence, and we will not fill it.

citation_entries.sentence: Paula set herself to learning Hebrew, and succeeded so well that she could chant the psalms in it without a Latin accent.

uncited_claim_sentences: That was not a ceremony we describe.
Paula's own children are said to have stood on the shore weeping as her ship left for the Holy Land.
She did not look back.
That was the scale of it.
Once at Bethlehem, what we can show is a life shaped by scriptural labor and discipline together.
The translation work - turning the books of scripture from Hebrew into Latin, which Jerome undertook alone - stood at the center of it.
Her daughter learned it after her.
Work for the hands.
The record we have is the record of the visible, the named, the ones whose wealth made the place and whose learning was its witness.
